content: Polyhydramnios, also known as polyhydramnion or hydramnios, is a medical condition characterized by an excessive accumulation of amniotic fluid within the amniotic sac. This condition occurs in approximately 5% to 2% of pregnancies. The opposite condition, oligohydramnios, involves a deficiency of amniotic fluid and is considered very rare. The etiology of polyhydramnios is often linked to maternal diabetes, accounting for about 20% of cases. In such instances, maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which in turn causes fetal polyuria. Since fetal urine is a major contributor to the amniotic fluid, this results in an overproduction of amniotic fluid. Additionally, around 20% of polyhydramnios cases are associated with fetal anomalies that impair the fetus's ability to swallow amniotic fluid. Normally, the fetus swallows amniotic fluid and absorbs it through the intestinal villi. Conditions that disrupt this process include: Gastrointestinal abnormalities, such as esophageal atresia and duodenal atresia, which obstruct the normal passage of swallowed fluid. Chromosomal abnormalities, such as Down syndrome, which is frequently associated with gastrointestinal defects. Neurological abnormalities, such as anencephaly, which impair the swallowing reflex. In pregnancies involving multiple gestations, twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome is a common cause of polyhydramnios. Fetuses affected by polyhydramnios are at an increased risk of complications, including umbilical cord prolapse, placental abruption, and perinatal death. At the time of delivery, it is essential to evaluate the newborn for congenital abnormalities. Treatment for polyhydramnios may involve amnioreduction in certain cases. This procedure reduces the volume of amniotic fluid to alleviate symptoms and mitigate risks associated with the condition.
